To enhance it, we propose a novel strategy called Pseudo-Ensemble Pseudo-Labeling (PEPL). PEPL leverages a Peeling-and-Translating (P&T) algorithm to generate multiple translations of a single target image, then ensembles their predicted labels. We conducted extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, showing the PEPL algorithm's superiority over existing methods in peeling noisy pseudo-labels. Notably, PEPL achieved a notable 9.1% increase in target data accuracy compared to standard pseudo-labeling. Furthermore, it showcased remarkable robustness, outperforming competitors by 29.5% in accuracy under high noise conditions. The accompanying code is available on GitHub.

This study examines the link between ionized hydrogen regions and a specific type of stellar region in the spiral galaxy UGC 8839, utilizing data from the Arecibo Legacy Fast Radio Burst project and previously catalogued properties of these stellar regions. By analyzing the connection between ionized hydrogen and young stellar clusters, we aim to understand the formation of these components within spiral galaxies. Our analysis takes into account various factors, including the potential for misclassified sources, and considers both empty time bins and those containing significant BAO signals when testing for correlations. The results indicate a moderate correlation between GRB afterglow optical light curves and the distance from the galactic center, suggesting that star formation in UGC 8839 follows a similar pattern. Additionally, the study reveals differences in the distribution of ionized hydrogen regions along the plane of the galaxy when compared to other studies, possibly indicating an underlying spiral arm structure. We also investigate the formation of ionized hydrogen regions and KS regions within UGC 8839, considering its spiral structure, and compare the regions' properties to those of other spiral galaxies.

The study of sub-GeV dark matter is being significantly influenced by emerging paleo-detector findings that define sensitive boundaries on interaction cross-sections, typically in the 10-eV to 100-eV mass range. These results are also affected by various factors including various dark matter scattering mechanisms, potential invisible decays of the dark photon, and alternative models such as the axion-like and "Galactic" dark photon scenarios. An innovative approach has been developed to integrate outputs from different scattering models with existing experimental constraints from paleo-detector experiments, and it's predicted that these studies will be capable of delineating more precise safe zones for future investigations, possibly down to cross-sections of 10^-49 cm^2/cm^2 by DUNE.

Modern databases, including social media and online reviews, generate complex, historical data updates as a result of increased user interactions and transactions. These data histories can disclose sensitive information, forcing a compromise between enriching analytics applications and protecting privacy. The emergence of differential privacy allows the efficient processing of massive datasets without over-emphasizing the contributions of individual users. Although research on differential history-aware data release is an active field, existing studies on this topic are limited to simplistic models that assume independent contributions and known update histories from all other users. No studies have addressed the problem of releasing differential history-aware data in a decentralized environment where individual users' full data contributions remain unknown. To fill this gap, we develop the first model for computing differential history-aware data in a decentralized setting and propose the first algorithm for achieving this goal. Moreover, we analyze the properties of differential history-aware data and investigate how the chosen differential privacy parameters and known data parameters influence the proposed algorithm. Furthermore, we examine the impact of choosing specific noise mechanisms and present several real-world applications of the proposed model and algorithm.

In our research, we have identified a distinct approach to evaluating the importance of features within machine learning models, particularly in the context of classification tasks in linear spaces. This method is rooted in infeasibility reasoning in linear programming and specifically focuses on Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores (MUCs). Our concept of a Minimal Unsatisfiable Core explains how a linear classifier utilizes linear inequalities derived from training data to eliminate certain regions of the feature space. If the MUC is small, it suggests that particular features are crucial for model predictions. To assess a feature's significance, we developed a score based on the frequency of its appearance in Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores across a test set. This score enables us to determine whether a specific feature is contributing positively, neutrally, or hindering the model's performance. If a test instance and a training instance belong to different classes, and a feature is present in the MUC defining this difference, it can be considered relevant. To validate our approach, we applied it to two publicly available datasets in our experiments, and the results showed that MUC-based feature importance outperformed other methods, and had a direct correlation with the coefficients assigned by the solver. Notably, this approach is model-agnostic and can be applied to any linear solver.

This study examines the challenges of using automated segmentation for surgical instruments during laparoscopic surgery. We analyze various Deep Learning methods to determine their suitability for this task and introduce an innovative approach called the Dual decoder attention network (DDANet). Our experiments show that DDANet outperforms other methods, achieving a significant improvement in segmentation accuracy for surgical instruments. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through extensive testing on a comprehensive dataset consisting of over 13000 surgical images, yielding a substantial increase in Intersection over Union metrics.

Deep learning techniques for real-world ReID have significant progress, but there's still room for improvement, particularly with limited or no annotated data. This study explores the use of contrastive learning in real-world ReID, focusing on two key aspects: unsupervised and metric learning ReID. For unsupervised ReID, we developed a new protocol and found that a simple contrastive loss function outperformed more complex alternatives. Our proposed unsupervised ReID method achieved remarkable results, particularly when combined with our new protocol. Similarly, for metric learning ReID, we demonstrated that a basic contrastive learning approach surpasses more complex methods, even when using pre-trained ReID models. These findings emphasize the superiority of the contrastive framework for ReID, highlighting the effectiveness of our proposed strategy.

We develop a general framework to create robust, translation-invariant GARCH models of value-at-risk that remain effective even when model assumptions are flawed. Our method yields flexible VA R specifications capable of capturing complex market behaviors like non-Gaussian distributions and multiple GARCH model effects, while delivering simpler, more accurate risk forecasts. Our study demonstrates the framework's superiority over conventional GARCH models for equities, fixed income, and alternative investments such as currencies, commodities, and market risk factors. Additionally, our results show the new framework's potential to significantly reduce GARCH framework's translation-invariance shortcoming, making it an improvement over GARCHVA R in various asset classes.

Using next-generation radio telescopes like SKA1, we can significantly improve our understanding of the pulsar timing array parameter space by employing advanced Bayesian inference methods. Comparing various sampling techniques, we find that nested sampling and affine-nested sampling are more effective than MCMC for exploring this parameter space. Affine-nested sampling, in particular, proves to be 100 times faster than MCMC in detecting a gravitational wave signal from inspiraling supermassive black hole binaries. We can also apply these algorithms to analyze the combined data sets of PTA collaborations, and potentially detect deviations from standard gravitational wave spectra or over-densities in the stochastic signal. Furthermore, we can use Bayesian model comparison to evaluate multiple waveform models and determine the most likely explanation for the observed data.

Using the MIQET framework, we apply a power-law ansatz for quark mass dependencies to evaluate the quark mass impacts on hadronic properties. For "safe" observables like pion mass and quark mass, we utilize Lattice QCD data to characterize these interactions. Our three-dimensional quark-matrix-analogy quantum electrodynamics framework then leverages this two-quark information to model four-quark states, specifically resonances. As a test, we check the resonance's response to changes in the quark mass. Comparing these predictions with Lattice QCD results shows a clear match, confirming the validity of our approach and the feasibility of applying quantum field theory to simulate scattering and form factors that lead to resonance formation.

Classical T Tauri stars exhibit significant fluctuations in accretion rates over both short and long time periods.  Detailed modeling of the disk around IN Mon, a C7 type classical T Tauri star, revealed that its variable infrared emission cannot be solely attributed to changes in accretion rates.  Instead, our research demonstrates that extreme fluctuations in accretion rates - varying by up to four orders of magnitude within a year - are necessary to explain the observed behavior of this system.  However, such findings contradict established theories of disk evolution which generally foresee decreasing accretion rates as the disk matures.  As a result, our research suggests that the extreme variability seen in classical T Tauri stars may be linked to turbulent processes occurring within viscous accretion disks.

Understanding the complex nature of luck's impact on people's finances is essential in shaping their attitudes toward redistribution. This study utilizes two economic models to explore how different forms of luck influence public opinion on redistribution. The first model shows that luck can affect opportunities, which in turn determine income, while the second model has luck directly determining income. Through experiments with 500 participants using an online platform, researchers discovered that public willingness to redistribute income is significantly higher when luck affects opportunities than when it directly determines income. This finding holds true even when individuals' actual earnings are determined by luck in the latter experiment. The results also vary depending on whether individuals believe they are more affected by luck than others, especially when luck affects opportunities. This study contributes to our understanding of the role luck plays in shaping people's attitudes towards equality and the principles of egalitarianism.

This study seeks to extend a prior proof by Li and Zhang, which established a connection between stable maps varieties and quantum K-invariants of a bundle over a vector space through an elliptic orbifold. We aim to demonstrate that this connection holds for the Grassmannian as well.

Debugging data pipelines is crucial, especially in pipelines that involve pipeline operations, where issues can be intricate and time-consuming to identify due to numerous possible data transformations. As data pipelines expand in size and scope, the risk of introducing issues also grows, underscoring the need for an efficient method of detecting problems in data pipelines. This paper introduces DataScope, a data debugger that leverages visualizing the effects of individual data transformations to facilitate the efficient detection and correction of issues in machine learning pipelines. DataScope enables developers to visually interact with pipeline operations and data flows by introducing the concept of slice operations, which isolate and visualize the intermediate data of machine learning pipelines from various angles. Furthermore, DataScope introduces the side car platform that allows programmers to visually compare the effects of individual data transformations, a core feature of data debugging, by introducing the scope operation, which is then utilized in data debugging tasks such as finding issues in a single machine learning pipeline, narrowing down the search for issues in a machine learning pipeline, and validating corrections to a machine learning pipeline. Evaluations of DataScope on real-world cases demonstrate its superiority to baseline approaches in terms of reducing the time required for pipeline repair while also improving the accuracy of the solutions found.

Researchers have posited that some globular clusters may host entire galactic nuclei, consisting of a bulge, disk, and even a supermassive black hole within their dynamical influence. To test this hypothesis, we examined the structure of 12 clusters with detected active radio sources located at their centers. Our analysis employed the Generalized Gaussian Model to dissect the shape of the radio emission surrounding these clusters and discovered 6 instances where the radio morphology aligns with the spatial distribution of the stellar component - purely generic, and not indicative of any neutron star or black hole identities. Notably, we found evidence of several millisecond pulsars within the core of the globular clusters, as well as potential neutron star X-ray binaries, supporting our previous assertions that some globular clusters may indeed resemble active galactic nuclei in miniature.

A major issue in analyzing network data is the reconstruction of hypergraphs from their projected views. Unfortunately, standard approaches for rebuilding graphs from their projections often fail to accurately restore the original hypergraph due to the absence of crucial information about individual hyperedges. This lack of data becomes especially pronounced as the number of dimensions decreases. To address this challenge, we have developed an innovative method that utilizes local representations to rebuild the hypergraph based on its hyperedge components. Our proposed method, reconstructing the incidence matrix through an alternating minimization process, can be efficiently solved with reasonable precision and has an efficient runtime. Our method has been shown to outperform state-of-the-techniques in rebuilding hypergraphs from their projected views, particularly when there are a limited number of dimensions available.

We have developed a novel approach to analyze ultrafast, near-infrared lasers with extreme precision at a macro scale, making it possible to evaluate their divergence angle in the near direction. This method leverages spatial light modulation, non-linear optical effects, and detection techniques associated with visible light. When compared to conventional methods, our approach offers greater accuracy and can evaluate the extreme directional characteristics of lasers, such as those used in atomic physics, yielding results in agreement with expectations from experiments, as evidenced by the findings: 0.16±0.02 and 0.25±0.02 milliradians.

We have developed an analytical method to understand how coherent light interacts with systems of atoms and demonstrated its application by calculating key functions describing the scattering process. Our approach is easy to implement and efficient in computing correlation functions, making it possible to accurately model experiments and identify areas for improvement in theoretical models. Our method was used to explain a experiment where measured data was compared with an existing theoretical model, revealing discrepancies especially in functions that describe the scattering of light at oblique angles. Unlike these models, our model provides precise results in computational terms and can be easily adjusted to include more complex systems of atoms by including the effects of atomic ensemble inhomogeneity and light scattering. Furthermore, our model can be applied to predict the scattering of light from systems of atoms illuminated by two coherent light beams with different intensities and phases, which causes the system of atoms to scatter an interference pattern. We have developed and numerically solved master equations to understand this process more deeply. Interestingly, our results show that this process can be described more simply than previous models for systems of atoms illuminated by a single beam of light, which may have significant implications for understanding how light interacts with matter at a fundamental level.

Offline reinforcement learning is a cost-effective approach for training high-quality policies but is hindered by limited sample sizes and suboptimal pre-collected trajectories. One offline method uses self-generated trajectories for correction and improvement, yet its performance is severely limited by the inability to explore the state space due to locked past actions. We introduce Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT), a novel framework that allows each agent to use its own action history for better state space exploration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in multi-agent learning tasks, including a multi-room navigation scenario and a multi-target shooting scenario, resulting in substantial performance gains of up to 222% over the existing state-of-the-art method.

This study proposes a novel approach for 3D-ACT image registration to 2D optical images, leveraging a deep learning framework. By incorporating label propagation and convolutional layers, the proposed method automatically generates intensity transformations and corresponding vector fields, ensuring one-to-one mappings between images. Comparison with traditional registration methods shows the proposed model's superior performance, particularly in scenarios with significant image misalignments. Furthermore, the proposed approach outperforms a state-of-the-art approach but is susceptible to boundary discontinuities when registering highly misaligned images.

A long-standing dispute concerns whether a single particle can be entangled, especially in contexts like nonlocal correlations, quantum steering, and Bell's theorem. We resolve this debate by showing that a single particle can indeed be entangled, particularly when it interacts with local environments. We introduce an approach based on quantum states that can be factorized or separated into products, allowing us to quantify single-particle entanglement and its nonlocal consequences. This method enables us to demonstrate the emergence of nonlocal effects and Bell inequality violations following local interactions, even when the resulting state appears local. Moreover, this framework allows us to measure the degree of single-particle entanglement and nonlocality in practical scenarios, such as when a neutral atom with a spin degree of freedom undergoes local interactions.

The Internet of Vehicles (IoV) is rapidly growing, offering numerous advantages but also posing significant security challenges. The IoV faces critical issues related to the authenticity, integrity, and privacy of shared data. To address these challenges, a blockchain-based solution has been proposed, leveraging the cryptographic properties and decentralized nature of blockchain technology for secure and private data management in IoV systems. The proposed system, referred to as BlockIoV, builds upon existing blockchain frameworks such as Ethereum, enhancing them with improved security, low-latency Vehicle to Everything (V2X) communication, and real-world applicability. BlockIoV introduces a new transaction type, called Parked-Service, that enables IoV users to outsource computational tasks to neighboring vehicles and compensate them accordingly. The design of BlockIoV follows the ISO/IEC 24730 standard for cryptographic application and has been evaluated through practical implementation and performance testing, including outcome accuracy and overall system efficiency.

A type of variable star known as a Nova Recurrenti has been identified in the constellation Perseus since 2022. Initial observations using the Swift-UVOT and the Chandra X-ray Telescope have been conducted to collect in-depth data on this celestial body. The findings reveal that upon a recent nova explosion, an explosive outflow from the star didn't completely settle back into place for at least a hundred days. Moreover, the receding flow from V392 exhibited an unusually high rate of decline within the X-ray spectrum, suggesting that the accretion disk surrounding it possessed a particularly thick and massive structure. This observed phenomenon supports the idea that V392 Persei was still in the stage of a heavy accretion disk when it entered its high-state of mass intake, thus providing unique insights into this type of recurrent nova system and enhancing our understanding of their explosive cycles.

As quantum processors advance, evaluating the quality of quantum gate operations becomes increasingly critical, especially for national leaders in quantum computing research.  Using error correction codes, we can assess code quality on quantum processors and develop more effective strategies for evaluating and comparing their performance.  A key element in evaluating code quality is developing scalable methods for accurate error measurement.  Here we examine the trade-offs between our ability to measure code performance and the complexity of these measurement protocols, comparing different approaches, before focusing on a quantum circuit that can be efficiently implemented on existing processors, with minimal overhead, and suitable for code quality evaluation of middle-sized processors.  A theoretical analysis of this approach is provided, with simulated results demonstrating its practicality in assessing code quality for processors with up to 50 qubits.

This research examines the use of feedback encoding in optical networks employing bidirectional clustering and provides a mathematical framework for designing an optimal encoding scheme. We demonstrate that a proposed feedback encoding method outperforms traditional Lloyd algorithms by providing nearly 30 times greater efficiency in pilot overhead while maintaining nearly 99.99 percent accuracy in user profile representation. We also examine the potential impact of quantization on power control performance and discuss potential applications of the proposed encoding scheme in practical implementations.

The concept of geometric phase is widely applied across multiple disciplines, yet its related concept of surface currents lacks a similar broad acceptance. Despite this, we show that surface currents represent a robust phenomenon that holds significant relevance for both bosonic and fermionic systems. The durability of quantum states, whether they are edge or pump states, is facilitated by surface currents. Surface currents can generate topological quantum numbers and diverence-free charge accumulations, all of which contribute to the characterization of materials. The surface currents' robustness is further supported by connections to the vacuum entanglement and photon decay rates. These cross-disciplinary links suggest that surface currents may serve as a crucial tool for the development of topological quantum devices.

In a massless scalar-tensor theory that lacks photons, we investigate the conditions under which the metric remains globally hyperbolic and allows light to reach infinity, despite the presence of escaping scalar radiation. Using a $2+2$ decomposition, we analyze a general class of Brans-Dicke theory and establish both necessary and sufficient conditions for light to reach infinity as long as the product of the theory's parameter $\omega$ and the initial scalar radiation power is greater than 36. This finding is then specialized for asymptotically flat and isolated horizon scenarios.

Due to a lack of heavy elements in the early universe, Population III (Pop III) stars died quickly, potentially leaving behind numerous compact objects like black holes, neutron stars, and white dwarfs. To understand when and where these Object Object (OO) mergers were most common, we utilized a method that accounts for the evolving populations of Pop III stars as the universe matured. Our model incorporated various mass ranges of Object Object (OO) binaries, considering their individual masses as well as the mass distribution within each range. Our findings show that the merger density reached its highest point in the universe's early stages, specifically 480 million years after the Big Bang, with an estimated rate of $1.06 \times 10^{-2}$ per gigaparsec cubed per year. We observed the peak merger rates occurring within a specific mass range of binary systems, characterized by two components with masses of $12.5 M_{\odot}$ and $15.6 M_{\odot}$, as well as a third binary system consisting of $0.8 M_{\odot}$ and $0.75 M_{\odot}}$ components. Our research highlights the potential for future third-generation gravitational wave detectors to differentiate between mergers originating from Pop III stellar remnants and those from higher population III stellar stages.

We have developed a Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) simulator, which is utilized by the Swift satellite's Virtual Observatories (SVO) for the BAT and XRT instruments, to create synthetic data that closely mimics real high-energy bursts. This simulator forms the foundation for VOO's validation and quality assurance (including the time jitter of 0.43 seconds for the BAT, which is significantly shorter than previously achieved times).

A specific type of operator, the composition-adjoint product $C_g$ on various submanifolds of a complex plane shape known as a Schur class, has been thoroughly investigated, resulting in clear criteria for its compactness, weak compactness, and complete reducibility. However, on manifolds with $1 < p < 2$, both weak and non-surjective compactness properties do not follow from the compactness of the generator $T_g$. This study establishes a direct link between the sup-norm and blockability of a generator under $\omega_p$ weights when considering the weak compactness of $C_g$ on $\omega_p$ classes within this $1 < p < 2$ weight range. Ultimately, this relationship allows both conditions for weak compactness of $C_g$ on $\omega_p$ classes to be expressed using a single, unified formula.

The evolution of scientific knowledge can be likened to a complex system of living entities that undergo continuous transformation, ultimately leading to new breakthrough discoveries. Although various concepts such as scientific impact factor and citation counts are commonly employed to assess a journal's influence, these metrics may not accurately reflect the progression of knowledge within a particular field of study. In contrast, our proposed index, the QQI, is designed to measure the flow of knowledge within literature, enabling us to determine the level of understanding within a particular field over time. Furthermore, the flexible nature of the QQI allows it to be applied to individual research articles, journals, databases, and even customized collections. As an extension, we explore the application of the QQI to the ArXiv database, a prominent repository for computer science literature, revealing intriguing temporal patterns within the discipline. Specifically, our analysis uncovers notable fluctuations in knowledge levels across various subfields of computer science, characterized by distinct phases of knowledge acquisition, reinforcement, and redefinition. Interestingly, the ArXiv results also expose an intriguing discrepancy: there is a significant gap in knowledge development between highly cited articles and the broader literature, indicating that citation frequency does not necessarily drive the growth of knowledge within a field of study.

This paper analyzes an information sharing system, where two nodes collaborate to transmit data to a third node in the presence of an unauthorized listener, using an amplify and forward technique. We develop a novel security evaluation metric that accounts for the different transmission strengths at each node and can also assess the impact of unauthorized access. Our research identifies optimal power distribution strategies that maximize secure data transmission, both generally and specifically for equal access scenarios, utilizing efficient mathematical optimization methods.

To create nonlocal quantum correlations, we propose using quantum emitters linked to topologically-protected edge modes in Weyl semimetallic nanotubes. By coupling these emitters to the edge modes, we can generate highly entangled states, such as single and double photon Fock states, with consistent efficiency and wavelength. The coherence of these states is protected due to the topological nature of the wire, resulting in multiple orders of magnitude longer lifespans compared to quantum emitters in other scenarios. Our model demonstrates the feasible detection of single and double photons, as well as their quantum correlations, and our study reveals the impact of Weyl node separation on the emitters' interaction with the edge modes and the resulting state longevity.

This research focuses on how traffic lights impact the decision-making process of connected automated vehicles navigating through urban intersections. Although previous studies have extensively covered the impact of basic traffic light information on CAVs, they have overlooked the specific effect of traffic light phases, particularly yellow and red phases, on CAVs' decision-making processes. To begin with, we collect public data on the movement of real-world vehicles during various phases of traffic lights and analyze their behavior, which reveals a tendency for cars to stop more frequently during yellow and red phases, even when there is ample time to come to a halt. To address this issue, we then develop a multi-objective path-finding problem for connected automated vehicles that takes into account the impact of traffic light phases, and design an efficient algorithm to generate initial solutions for this problem.

Interactive learning techniques, like text-based learning games, utilize vast amounts of simulated experience data to accomplish complex goals. Generating huge datasets normally requires slow sampled policies and result in inefficient training. We've developed a highly efficient text-based environment simulator called TextWorldExpress for Python that achieves 200 times faster sampling than the previous method. This high-speed TextWorldExpress environment has been employed to train models for the Mastermind game, resulting in a remarkable 4 times improvement in performance and also showcasing significant gains of up to 200 times faster solving speeds of 100 times 100 boards compared to prior sampled-based methods.

Recent advancements in deep learning have transformed oriented model hardware design,
particularly for tensor operations like convolutions and dilated convolutions.
Although these methods enhance hardware efficiency, they introduce significant memory
access overhead during dense matrix multiplication, the primary computation in Tensor
Networks (TNs). We introduce a novel TN processing architecture, a fused Dilated
Hartley Transform Long Short-Term Memory (FDHT-LSTM), utilizing the FT/LHT
transform to replace dense matrix multiplication with efficient sparse calculations.
Benchmarking our FDHT-LSTM design shows improvements of up to $7.2\times$ and $3.2\times$
over conventional tensor-decomposed hardware models, achieving gains in speed,
throughput, energy efficiency, and storage usage.

This treatise explores cutting-edge data augmentation techniques in NLP, focusing on
distillation, synonym replacement, back-translation, and paraphrased datasets.
Our analysis is grounded in findings from recent empirical studies on current top
models, particularly in instruction learning, classification, and machine translation.
We examine the effects of various data augmentation methods on performance, especially
with limited data, and explore the potential of combining multiple techniques for better
results. This summary will remain relevant until proven otherwise by future studies.

For theories that support stable vacuums in anti-de Sitter space, extending the Weak Gravity Conjecture to include self-binding statements is possible. This can be accomplished by formulating a single inequality that incorporates the standard four-vector form of the WGC, minimizing the self-energy to its absolute lower limit relative to the charge. This minimum self-energy limit is determined by either a local form of the WGC or by the swampland distance conjecture, depending on the specific theoretical framework. Our study in anti-de Sitter space reveals that self-binding interpretations, although seemingly varied, ultimately boil down to essentially the same principle and can be understood as different expressions of a more fundamental concept, akin to a "family" of expressions for a singular idea. This forms the basis for what we term the "Strong" version of the Weak Gravity Conjecture. We apply this formulation to both supergravity and models containing scalar fields that are in compliance with the cosmological Einstein gravity, and we demonstrate that binding statements are mutually consistent with these models. We also propose an alternative interpretation of the $\text{AdS}_5$ $R^2$ inflation model that adheres to both the Weak and Cosmic Conjectures. This study is an extension of our previous work that examined the implications of the WGC in anti-de Sitter space, specifically in relation to its conflict with self-binding statements.

QuantumMonteCarlo methods face a challenging issue related to the estimation of multiple desired states within a many-body wave function, exacerbated by sign problems. To better estimate several states simultaneously within a simulation, we have developed a new approach that groups states into 'clusters' in the Hilbert space. This method has been successfully applied to various systems, including exact-spectrum benchmarks for H$_2$ and LiH molecules, as well as systems with significant degeneracy such as the half-filled 2D t-J model and the NiO system. Especially in cases with strong degeneracy, we have observed that our method can efficiently estimate multiple state clusters with low statistical fluctuations and minimal bias.

Let's consider a univariate polynomial $A$ with coefficients in the integers and an integer $a$ that is not divisible by three. In this context, a local ring is said to be non-F-rational if and only if a specific subset, which describes the elements of a particular group that vanish under repeated application of a derivative operator, is infinitely large. Additionally, it has been established that this infinite subset can be characterized by a more manageable expression involving the application of a derivative operator to a related, reduced form of $A$ at a point where three to the power of $a$ is congruent to zero (modulo three to the power of $a$ plus two).

This paper modelled the European electricity market with the inclusion of a day-ahead dispatch market, known as redispatch, using a game theory approach. A game was developed in which the market participants, generators, had influence over the marginal prices at different grid locations, while the grid operator, as the leader, could set the redisdispatch area boundaries. Analysis of this game showed the operator's optimal strategy was an all-or-nothing order design, either selecting a single node or encompassing the entire planning region. Simulations suggested that this design could result in higher costs for the operator, increased generation prices, and marginally lower consumer bills.

A key finding from this research is that for a field $K$ with characteristic zero or large enough positive integer characteristic, and its algebraic extension $K$, given any collection of prime numbers in $K$, there exists a specific Galois group within $S_n(K)$ that matches the specified collection while also ensuring the smallest set of invariant elements corresponds to a specific irreducible polynomial with a particular growth in degree as the number of primes increases. This conclusion implies the existence of a particular irreducible polynomial with a particular growth in degree, for which the Galois group matches that of the specified collection of primes and it also breaks a potential hypothesis linked to the Bateman-Horn conjecture and Milne's inquiry, and it also allows for this match to be a symmetric group or a specific type of linear group for any collection of primes that meets certain conditions and it also permits this match to be an alternating group in certain circumstances.

Our sensitivity to new physics at the LHC is significantly impacted by the need to precisely measure the background at this energy scale. Consequently, any modification to the background that follows a power law can be detected as a signal for new physics. Due to the difficulty in theoretically predicting the background with high precision in certain regions of phase space, our ability to identify such deviations is quite limited. Therefore, the cross section for top quark pair production must match the predicted value within a certain percentage, or the corresponding energy precision required is several times the expected threshold. This finding underscores the critical role that the accuracy of background knowledge and the precision of fundamental parameters like alpha_s will have on our search for new physics through direct or indirect means at the LHC.

In models with additional scalar sectors, such as two-Higgs-doublet models, we investigate how precise, zero-energy-transfer scattering and detailed Higgs properties can provide the most stringent tests, particularly when new scalar particles are heavy. Focusing on the Standard Model extension with one additional doublet, we found that combining the diphoton decay rate measurement at zero uncertainty and zero-beta term yields a lower bound on the heavy scalar Higgs boson mass of 645 GeV. Similarly, with just the central value of the diphoton decay rate, the lower mass limit is 540 GeV. Similarly, combining zero-energy-transfer data and Higgs coupling measurements, the lower mass limit is 825 GeV. 5 LHC run can further reduce this bound by approximately 50 GeV. If heavy scalar Higgs bosons are discovered, it will enable direct exploration of the scalar potential, likely leading to the discovery of additional scalar particles.

This research focuses on the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV), which exists at Saturn's north pole during the summer of 2019. Unlike the polar stratospheric features observed at Saturn's south pole during the same season, which are typically scattered and quiescent, the NPSV is characterized by a dense, high-pressure area that is both stable and distinct. Through data from various sources, including the Cassini spacecraft's final orbits and NASA's Juno mission, we have obtained wind measurements and temperature data for the North Pole. Additionally, simulations using the GCM model have further enhanced our understanding of this unique phenomenon. While visiting the South Pole during the winter of 2004-2005, the SOIR instrument on the Hubble Space Telescope recorded wind velocities of approximately 100 m/s at the edge of the planet, which is much slower than the velocities observed at the edge of the North Pole, which are around 200 m/s.

We investigate solutions to the Schrödinger equation within a bounded domain, focusing on a subcritical range of parameters. In subcritical parameters, solution norms increase with time due to the Milner-Kauppa effect, causing a finite-time singularity when an initial condition meets specific criteria. When the parameter is in a critical range, the situation changes, and the situation mirrors the behavior observed in whole space scenarios, where solutions exhibit polynomial growth in time and may exhibit an infinite-time singularity at a specific point in the domain with an unbounded norm at any positive time. When the parameter exceeds a certain critical range, the situation reverts to an expansion of the initial condition's norm. Our research fills a gap in the literature by analyzing boundary operator scenarios, excluding the scenario in which the parameter is above a certain critical range, where the situation already exhibits an increase of the initial condition's norm.

This study introduces two fresh perspectives in commutative algebra: positive-characteristic and characteristic-zero. Leveraging Galois theory, the relationship between these perspectives is explored through a summary of their key properties and interconnections, particularly focusing on the interplay between flat and integral morphisms and the behavior of determinants and discriminants in both characteristics. Additionally, certain aspects of this framework can be understood via a Galois-theoretic lens.

Our investigation into the spectral weight distribution in complex many-body electron systems has been extended based on previous findings by Basker and Huse. By deriving new rules relating a system's and its non-interacting counterpart's spectral weight distribution, we reveal how 'sum rules' for spectral weight typically apply with minor deviations. However, these deviations become significant during metal-insulator transitions in strongly correlated systems. Our new derived inequalities further constrain this phenomenon. To substantiate our theory, we apply it to analyze and compare the spectral weight distribution in a solvable 1D model and a 2D Bose-Hubbard model. In particular, we discover that the breakdown of these derived inequalities precisely pinpoints the 1D metal-insulator transition. Additionally, our research connects electron interaction strength to specific spectral features, such as electron-hole recombination energies. A similar strategy yields metal-insulator dividing lines for 1D and 2D models with bosonic on-site repulsion.

Researchers have used a numerical method to analyze a quantum system with two interacting density drops, or 'dark solitons', in a type of wave system known as the one-dimensional Gross-Itterovici equation. By accurately modeling the system, they were able to examine the structure of the quantum state, finding that it has a specific pattern: it has a low probability of occurrence in the middle and on the edges, with a higher probability in between. This state can be described as consisting of two quantum waves, or 'polaritons', interacting in the region where the density drops meet. Furthermore, the researchers discovered that there is a point where the boundary between the two drops becomes smooth, which indicates a unique property of the system known as rigidity. Their findings provide a detailed understanding of the behavior of the density drops and their internal quantum states.

A symplectical double vector bundle is a structure that combines a double vector bundle with a compatible symplectic form, similar to how a double Lie group is composed of a double Lie algebroid, which is a vector bundle whose both sides possess additional structure of a Lie algebroid. This concept was initially explored by C. Molino in 1980. Building on this, a triple Lie algebroid, which is a non-abelian generalisation, was defined by P. Xu in 1994. A double Lie algebroid is then a double vector bundle that is both a triple Lie algebroid and a symplectical double vector bundle that is perpendicular to both horizontal and vertical distributions. This concept was further developed by P. Xu in 1995. This concept was initially explored in 1995 and a compatible symplectic form was introduced in 1995. A recent study examines the connection between geometric and Kirillov measures within Lie algebra coadjoint orbits, focusing on the implications of measure disintegration. By analyzing the geometry of certain orbital sets, the paper determines measures for subsets of specific orbits in sl2,C,x4, revealing a novel geometric structure for these subsets, which are shown to be isomorphic to a particular parabolic cylinder in another specific orbit, while also determining their geometric measure.

A challenge persists in x-ray scattering experiments at high energies when attempting to measure phase and reconstruct energy spectra from real-space intensity patterns. The existing method utilizing the Hilbert transform has limitations in accuracy for objects that do not follow a smooth curve. The proposed algorithm significantly enhances the resolution for features that vary on a short length scale. It is observed that the method is particularly effective in reconstructing the atomic positions in various molecules across multiple photon energy ranges. The algorithm also exhibits accuracy in the low-energy regions for areas such as water and carbon monoxide, and it is found that the details of the first few atomic shells in these objects can be recovered in real-space by analyzing the position of the first zero-crossing point. Furthermore, the algorithm is found to be effective in reconstructing objects in the near-zone by the use of an appropriate approximation of the wave field. A method is also developed that allows the removal of the source screen in the experiment. It is observed that the phase plate is not necessary for the accurate reconstruction of objects when the appropriate algorithm is applied to far-field data.

A key aspect of quantum error correcting codes is the presence of a disordered classical state, similar to those studied in disordered statistical mechanics models. By studying the application of the transfer matrix method to the Ising model on a 1D lattice, this study demonstrates that simple quantum states, subject to local measurements, are related to the marginal probabilities of classical spin arrangements. Furthermore, it establishes a connection between the entanglement entropy of these measured systems and the entropy of the resulting classical spin pairs, ultimately facilitating the calculation of von Neumann entanglement entropy for a specific code, utilizing the exact solution of a classical disorder-affected system.

We investigate the electronic properties of various types of tellurene quantum wells using first-principles calculations. Initial analysis focuses on how lattice strain and quantum-confinement effects influence the band structure, demonstrating that a significant energy gap of approximately 0.3 ecan be opened through strain engineering in type-I tellurene quantum wells with an energy range of 0 to 0.3 eV. Furthermore, by applying lightht and heavy hole effective masses along with a material parabolic band approximation, we determine the cyclotron effective mass and light-hole/heavy-hole mass ratio for different quantum-well configurations. Additionally, our study examines how quantum confinement and strain impact the optical properties, particularly the binding energy and oscillation frequency of carrier excitations within these tellurene quantum wells.

A new approach is presented for simulating flow through complex networks of fractures in media with varying porosity. The network model accounts for the interaction between flow within fractures and flow through the surrounding rock matrix. The blocking of fractures is modeled using a Dirac-$\beta$ function with an exponent that varies over time. To determine this exponent, an energy-based method is used, which considers two key factors: the surface area of the new fracture surface and the energy required to break the rock's bonds. This approach allows for the identification of the new factor m in Dirac's distribution as 1/4. The model also enables us to observe how the new parameter m influences the mean time it takes for the network to become completely isolated.

A new class of materials, spin-valves, has been identified in ferrimagnetic alloys of Lanthanum and Transition metals, offering a pathway to manage high magnetization at low energy costs. Our theoretical analysis reveals that these spin-valves exhibit unusual behavior under moderate magnetic fields, where fields can efficiently flip the spin state. Observing this phenomenon, we utilized a novel structure, a Ferromagnetic layer paired with the ferrimagnetic alloy, to leverage the magnetic control of high magnetization. Our Kohn-Sham calculations indicate that very low exchange fields can achieve spin-state transition, which could significantly reduce the energy costs of data storage. However, incorporating a small unidirectional anisotropy allows for increased exchange fields, thus striking a balance between low energy operation and stable spin states.

In formal decision-making, choosing a course of action relies on a predefined set of options and evaluation criteria. However, in less structured scenarios like scientific discovery, there's no established framework for assessing the validity of hypotheses. To address this challenge, we view hypothesis selection as a decision problem and propose a utility function that earmarks resources for verifying the chosen hypothesis. This approach enables learning the most effective strategy to balance the chosen hypothesis with anticipated performance. Notably, this method can adapt to changes in the cost of verification and theoretical assumptions connect it to context-based evaluation models. Through simulations, we demonstrate its practicality in discovering suitable hypotheses.

The effective comprehension and production of spoken language relies heavily on Pairs of Connected Speech Acts (PCCS), which are formed by connected utterances that use discourse markers to create specific semantic relationships. Although numerous datasets exist that cover individual aspects, such as mentioned utterances, their scarcity hampers the development of models capable of capturing the interconnected nature of speech acts. In response, we introduce the dataset 'DiscSense', which addresses this scarcity by covering the full spectrum of semantic connections between utterances, including a wide array of discourse markers and their associated connections. Unlike other datasets, 'DiscSense' provides a comprehensive analysis of connected speech acts, including a range of utterance pairs that are both semantically and syntactically diverse. As a result, this dataset provides a comprehensive and nuanced exploration of the complexity of connected speech acts, including utterance pairs that are both semantically and syntactically diverse. Consequently, it serves as an essential resource for the creation of deeper, more semantically aware models of the intricacies of the many subtle semantic connections between utterances that are characteristic of human speech.

A simple formula for the energy barrier to nonradiative recombination in a SiP5 defect has been calculated using the Mott-Seitz model, found to be 2.04 eV. However, a previously reported higher barrier of over 2.4 eV cannot be explained by structural relaxation alone. It's suggested that nonadiabatic effects may be responsible, which could influence silicon spin qubit stability.

A novel algorithm for training multilayer perceptrons is outlined, establishing a general framework that encompasses both conventional backpropagation and the Jordan approach. We delve into the mechanism of error calculation at each network layer within the algorithm's framework and propose an alternative, mathematically based method. Through a series of straightforward cases, we compare the distinct error computation approaches and present the underlying theory. Finally, we address the computation of error signals in the network's hidden layers using the mathematical method and discuss the relationship between this approach and the application of normal equations for solving linear systems of equations.

A specific homeotopy property of the target space in a model for magnetic dynamics directly impacts the range of magnetic skyrmion sizes present. This requirement also dictates whether point-like or tube-like skyrmions can exist. By relaxing this condition, we find additional skyrmion configurations, ultimately leading to a classification of tube-like skyrmions based on a set of invariants. These results suggest different magnetic skyrmion formations can be created using various magnetic materials and exchange interactions.

Using a minimal basis set of s and p Gaussian functions, we have achieved a significant reduction in complexity for calculating the exact energy and all one- and two-electron properties of an s pd atom, by leveraging the symmetry of the system and averaging over the possible L values. This method can also be applied to any Gaussian basis set and is utilized in our study. A analysis of convergence to an exact value for any given electronic structure is performed, and we have found that when L is large, Hartree-Fock convergence is substantially influenced by the Coulomb interaction's magnitude, even more so than the exchange interaction, which is surprisingly accounted for by purely basis-set effects at fixed L. The feasibility of using a limited Gaussian basis set to accurately model high-L states of hydrogen-like atoms is demonstrated, which can be relevant for analyzing certain cometary and astrophysical spectra.

This study investigates a sudden onset of synchronization in systems with irregular
connections and synchronization dynamics, mirroring research on network structures that
rapidly disconnect from their equilibrium state. We analyze an array of phase-based
network nodes that undergo explosive synchronization, avoiding hysteresis and
phase coexistence through careful examination of both network topology and dynamics. Our
findings across various model systems reveal that explosive synchronization is possible
when there's a strong correlation between dynamic and structural discrepancies,
proposing an index of mean absolute adaptability to evaluate this interplay. Our
approbe has significant implications for researching other sudden transitions in
systems with discrete network dynamics and connections.

This paper examines a class of optimization problems that involve Riemannian manifolds and linear mappings, commonly encountered in applications like low-rank optimization and phase retrieval on product manifolds. When dealing with strongly convex and smooth objectives embedded in a globally non-positive curvature manifold, we establish local strong geodesic convexity and smoothness conditions. Under these conditions, convergence rates are determined for Riemannian gradient methods, with specific considerations given to the use of linearized gradients. Additionally, we address the problem of minimizing folded objectives by solving a differential inclusion and demonstrating that the original problem can be equivalently reformulated as a constrained minimization task, ensuring unique global solutions. To further explore the local convergence characteristics, we develop sufficient conditions for restricted strong convexity and smoothness, with an emphasis on Grassmannian manifold factorization.

The strong chromatic edge index of a graph is defined as the minimum number of colors needed for edge coloring in which every pair of vertices is connected by different colored edges within a certain distance. In 1990, Faudree and Schelp made a conjecture about bipartite graphs with a low maximum degree, suggesting that such graphs only require a specific number of colors. This study proves that these graphs indeed meet this requirement by showing that they satisfy a higher capacity based on their degree, thus confirming a related theorem and conjecture. Additionally, two lower limits are established to help calculate the exact strong edge chromatic indices of certain graph types.

This article examines various identities concerning Dirichlet L-functions at the point of evaluation s=0. Notably, it derives equivalent forms of Gauss sums that connect to these identities, ultimately facilitating proofs of several relationships between classical Gauss sums and dirichlet L-functions.

Our conventional understanding of gravitational-wave backgrounds typically relies on the assumption of equilibrium among the different degrees of freedom in the early universe. These factors may cause significant deviations from our expectations, particularly during the scaling phase of the Hubble parameter. During this phase, we demonstrate that observing non-uniformity in the gravitational-wave background would offer a valuable insight into the nature of reheating and the thermalization of relativistic species following the inflationary period. We examine how non-equilibrium effects on gravitational-wave signals may be utilized as a probe of reheating, particularly when featuring multiple sources of violation of equilibrium. This is especially possible when the rate of decay of the inflaton field is modulated by the masses of the particles it interacts with, which is typical in scenarios where it decays into both heavy and light particles. This situation is typical of the curvaton inflation model. In such cases, we find that detecting peaks in the gravitational-wave background corresponding to the mass range of $10^{10}$ to $10^{12}$ GeV, which is typical of the curvaton mass range, could provide us with the opportunity to determine the scale of the Grand Unified Theory and the value of the curvaton field responsible for curvature perturbations. This is possible even when taking into account constraints from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and the amplitude of curvature perturbations.

We examine the time-dependent rotation of a helical structure moving through a viscous fluid using the low-Reynolds-number approximation from Stokes flow theory. Our analysis, validated experimentally by Quere in 2001, reveals the phenomenon of a snowman-like effect. This outcome directly impacts the swimming capabilities of the helix and explains why adding a spherical object to the helix's tip can enhance its forward movement. Our novel analytical approach accurately predicts time-dependent behaviors of a general helix, including those with asymmetric cross-sections, and our predictions are confirmed by direct numerical simulations.

This study investigates how quickly populations converge to a stable state using a co-evolutionary genetic algorithm when applied to a simple model with two possible outcomes, which is also an idealized example for studying complex evolutionary processes that lead to multiple outcomes and stagnation at a high-energy equilibrium. We utilize a model known as the anti-coordination game and compare performance under two optimization methods: a social learning scenario, in which the entire population updates simultaneously based on shared strategy success rates, and a individual learning case, in which each agent independently evaluates strategy payoffs before making its own updates. Our findings show that the speed of convergence to a stable equilibrium is primarily determined by a key parameter representing the relative change in payoffs per iteration, which represents the inverse of population size. We derive an analytical expression for large populations using a stochastic differential equation approximation, which we verify through numerical simulations even for smaller population sizes. Our results indicate that a social learning approach leads to quicker convergence than individual learning, due to reduced genetic drift in the social learning scenario.

To protect users on the dark web, the Tor browser relies on secure features within the code, necessitating efficient extraction of vulnerable concepts from source code comments. This study proposes an innovative term importance measurement technique, enabling accurate security concept extraction using Bidirectional LSTMs, and demonstrates its effectiveness on the Tor browser code, outperforming existing methods.

A variant of the voter model, incorporating two distinct magnetization values, is examined on an infinite, degree-degree homogeneous graph. This hybrid model simulates opinion interaction, where like-minded individuals influence each other more than dissimilar counterparts, drawing from a complete graph example. Analyzed using mean-field theory, this model's behavior is examined through a mapping to a bipartite system, ultimately showing that magnetization in this hybrid model is the square root of that in a pure Ising model. Furthermore, conditions are derived that guarantee the absence of bistability in this hybrid system. On the example of a tree, this research demonstrates the prevalence of multiple stable states, completing the investigation of binary opinion interaction mechanisms.
