Human-computer interaction (HCI) techniques that rely on computer vision often
have significant drawbacks, OTOH face-centered gaze detection (FGD) has nearly
zero training costs and provides a focused, intuitive approach. Building on these
advantages, this study introduces an eye-focused detection system (EFoD) that
pioneers gaze detection using only a portion of the eye, whereas traditional
gaze detection methods require the entire face. OTOH the EFoD model requires
more data for learning, whereas conventional FGD methods require only a small
amount. To address this challenge, EFoD has been assessed on two distinct setups:
one using a limited subset of eye images captured from a single user with the
task of directing the eye in various ways, and another using multiple users with
a limited sample per user. FGoD achieved higher accuracy in both scenarios,
whereas EFoD surpassed FGoD on the first test but required more training data
to excel in the second. These findings indicate that FGD may outperform EFoD in
specific applications, and that EFoD has the potential to be used in novel HCI
that involves directing the eye or part of it.

This study compares the robustness of determining a mass difference in a quark system when the quark has three possible states (a qutrit) versus two states (a qubit). Using a realistic model for measuring the energy gap between the qutrit's energy levels, our findings show that a qutrit experiment could give a more precise mass measurement by as much as five times the precision of a qubit experiment, assuming the noise levels are similar. However, if one type of noise heavily affects both energy gaps, the extra qudit level starts to be more tolerant to noise than a qubit, making mass determination more accurate. We also found that a simpler, three-level model actually makes the mass calculation less sensitive to noise compared to a more complicated four-level model. These results suggest using qutrits might be a step forward for future research even as more complex systems are being studied, such as a molecular system being noise-resistant to a significant degree, whereas other models, including a simulated four-level system, turned out to be quite sensitive to noise.

Our recent findings reveal that high-energy selection in a helical solenoid
magnet effectively increases the polarization of positrons to over 30%, a
breakthrough with potential implications for multiple projects including the muon
g-2, an E6 muon colliders, and a neutron electric dipole moment experiment.
By adapting the posac code, researchers calculated the required magnet length to
attain this level of polarization at various positron energies.
Our analysis also demonstrated that adjusting the selection angle can control
spin precession and minimize precession errors, and confirmed the feasibility
of this approach in the muon g-2 ring. This achievement in positron
polarization demonstrates the practicality of this method for upcoming E6 muon
colliders and neutron electric dipole moment experiments.

Groups that have polynomial diameter display rich structural characteristics. These groups feature finitely many nilpotent subgroups with a given order, a finite number of conjugacy classes within their own groups, and groups with polynomial diameter remain closed under taking commutators, subgroups, and quotients. In this project, we aim to expand upon existing results by exploring the properties of groups with polynomial diameter, including their Schur multipliers, extensions, and overlying Birkhoff-Witt groups.

This research focuses on an inverse problem, specifically on creating a compact and precise temperature measurement system using COTS sensors and a CPU, inverse modeling, and optimization techniques. In situations where a function maps temperatures to measurable frequencies, our group has developed an inverse function to estimate temperatures from those frequencies. Although the used sensors and CPU do not meet high-precision standards, our method successfully produced a highly accurate and resolution-driven temperature estimator. This successful experiment demonstrates the capability to create sophisticated inverse models using basic components, which in turn can lead to more efficiently functionally equivalent circuits with lower complexity requirements.

Magnetic fields in stars and planets are generated through a process called the dynamo, which involves a complex interaction between the dynamo and magnetohydrodynamics in a rotating, conducting fluid. A key question researchers are asking is whether mutually stabilizing toroidal and poloidal components of the magnetic field can lead to magnetic self-excitation without any external influence. To answer this question, they developed linear models for ideal MHD and found that small linearity breakages, such as at the boundary layers, can always lead to ideal MHD linearity instability, resulting in magnetic self-excitation. A newly discovered linear mode of growth has also been described in linearity unstable configurations, which can be applied to explain the sudden appearance of poloidal magnetic fields on the surface of Saturn's north pole.

When a system's Hamiltonian cannot be reversed in time, its corresponding renormalization group (RG) trajectory cannot be reversed either. A specific, non-local function of Hamiltonian parameters, first introduced by Fisher and Pelissetto in 1991, consistently increases along the RG flow and can be viewed as an entropy for the Hamiltonian. A connection has been established between the Wilsonian action's non-local term and the equilibrium properties of a class of holographic fluids with non-evolving sources, suggesting a connection between the non-equilibrium behavior of RG flows and the irreversibility of fluid dynamics. A hypothesis has been proposed stating that a suitable, non-local combination of the fluid's entropy and chemical potential might serve as an invariant for the fluid's energy-momentum tensor divergence, mirroring a relationship proposed by Witten between field theory and RG flow and the non-equilibrium dynamics of fluid dynamics. This proposed invariant has been calculated for specific, exact RG trajectories, including those of free scalar field theory and VTANH, with potential applications to the VTANH model's scattering amplitude. These findings may be applicable to the broader non-equilibrium dynamics of integrable quantum field theories.

When tasked with finding music lyrics or audio, individuals often rely on standard web searches, but these can be inefficient due to scattered and non-uniform presentation of results. To address this issue, we've developed MusicLyricsRetrieval, a new problem definition that aims to make the process of retrieving music lyrics or audio from search queries more straightforward. To facilitate this, we've created a large-scale dataset consisting of 100k real-world queries manually annotated by music enthusiasts and fans, along with their corresponding correct answers. Additionally, we've analyzed various subtypes of music lyrics queries and proposed specific methods to handle each. Our findings show that the majority of models struggle with music title entanglement and ambiguous artist names. We've also developed an innovative all-in-one music graph called MusicLyra, which enhances the music text-retrieval process through structured music name parsing and unam biguous artist identification. MusicLyra has achieved remarkable improvements, demonstrating up to a 21.5% gain in model accuracy in music text-retrieval tasks.

Given any topological groupoid having a product structure, we show that a specific type of topological groupoid extension corresponds to a particular kind of topological groupoid gerbe over that topological groupoid's underlying space. Additionally, our research establishes a topological version of a higher-category 2-morphism between 1-morphisms in a higher-category, which is equivalent to a topological groupoid 3-morphism being a specific type of topological groupoid object over that higher-category.

Observations of star formation in nearby galaxies often show a surprising relationship: core masses seem unrelated to how many or how large the stars that result are. To understand core to core variability and its effect on the mass of stars formed, we developed a model based on a detailed core evolution framework. This framework is then compared to existing data, which shows core mass growth in our simulations aligns closely with a linear pattern, core mortality rates are influenced by core structure rather than environment, and core lifespans are much longer than previously estimated. This discrepancy in mortality rates affects how we calculate the molecular gas to star conversion factor, making it appear faster in regions with shorter gas lifespans. However, molecular gas variability in different environments is better explained by the distribution of core life times rather than the distribution of core mortality rates. Ultimately, core mass growth is accelerated linearly over time, core death is often sudden, and the resulting core to star mapping is sub-linear, which may help reconcile the core data with the final star distribution observed in our simulations.

This study begins by representing Godel algebras as certain dynamic algebras based on finite forests, then characterizing them through finite bipointed forests preorders. Notably, it discovers a dual relationship where finite Godel algebras correspond to finite bipointed forests preorders.

A LiDAR classification task involving 3D point clouds is sensitive to classification labels being correctly assigned to neighboring points within the dataset. To address this issue, we propose an adaptive noise correction method that adjusts the classification decision for each point based on the distribution of neighboring point labels. This method is implemented using two models: a linear selection method and a deep learning-based method. Our experiments show that this method consistently improves the classification accuracy of imperfect datasets by 2.5%-6.2%, with particularly significant gains observed in under-performed classes. Furthermore, our context-based model outperformed existing enhancement methods that attempt to restore damaged features in incomplete datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling datasets with mislabeled points.

This study focuses on the preservation of posdefiniteness in functions defined on a class of elliptic operators, specifically looking at Jordan-Kleinian operators and their applications to positive-definite zonal functions on compact Riemannian manifolds with constant curvature. We establish relationships between functions of these operators and their derivatives with respect to these operators, and explore connections with positive-definite functions of related operators on the same manifolds. Notably, we have methods to determine the kernel of functions of second-order Kleinian-Gordon operators in both a compact symmetric space and its universal cover, which is a non-compact symmetric space. We also discuss potential relationships with the Bochner-Laplacian and heat kernel of a constant curvature manifold.

Recent research has suggested a strong connection between ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and high-energy neutrinos, positing that both are byproducts of the same ultra-high-energy cosmic accelerators. Given new observations of individual cosmic rays and significantly improved data on neutrino distributions, our reanalysis indicates that the current understanding is likely overestimated by a considerable margin - possibly tenfold. As a result, our revised models no longer predict neutrino fluxes exceeding existing experimental limits, and they offer a clearer explanation for the observed distributions of both cosmic rays and neutrinos. Specifically, our model effectively represents the current experimental data for both particle types and could potentially be verified with existing and upcoming data sets.

Investigating the influence of surface roughness on the dynamics of liquid foams is complicated, as even minor imperfections can significantly alter the foam's overall behavior. The roughness factor is defined as $r = w/d_0$, where $w$ represents the root-mean-square height variation and $d_0$ is the thickness of the foam's drainage channel. To investigate this, we constructed microscopically rough surfaces up to $r \approx 0.15$, using a precise sandblasting method. Our experiments involved releasing two D2O foams with varying $d_0$ onto these rough surfaces, utilizing high-speed video to record the resulting rebound. The observed total energy of the foam after impact was found to exceed that of an idealized $d_0$ by a factor of $r^{\\alpha}$, with $\\alpha \\approx 1.4$. This discovery indicates that our model of rebound is missing a crucial mechanism that becomes increasingly dominant as the degree of surface roughness rises.

Deep learning techniques have significantly improved, particularly in the field of image recognition. Nonetheless, these methods still face certain limitations. A common approach to overcoming these limitations is utilizing flat architectures. In contrast to this, a approach utilizing non-flat architectures has been proposed. Specifically, a method utilizing ensemble classifiers and a back-propagation learning algorithm to modify feature representations was demonstrated. This method was achieved by replacing the final fully connected layer with multiple classifiers, allowing for the calculation of a non-Euclidean distance metric in the feature space. Furthermore, a method to optimise the metric parameters via gradient descent was also illustrated, resulting in significant improvements to the classifier performance and the feature representations, as evaluated by downstream tasks and qualitative visualisation techniques such as t-SNE.

In a rotating Hele-Shaw cell filled with a demonstration fluid, the boundary between inside and outside states may exhibit various instabilities influenced by tension at the membrane. A simple model effectively captures the key features of multiple states by using an appropriate potential function. Notably, a sharp transition occurs between coexisting inside/outside states and ruffled states as membrane tension increases, while an gradual transition is observed when competing unstable states are involved. This phenomenon is explained by examining how these states are positioned relative to each other in an landscape. Additionally, heuristics can be used to predict coherent patterns of multiarm star shapes that arise when certain balance of forces. These theoretical models are supported by computer simulations and experimental validations using water and a surfactant mixture.

A new idea is proposed to resolve the contradiction between the resolvable work measured in experimental single-cell thermodynamics and the theoretically insurmountable work calculated in computer simulations. It is defined as an output microwork that occurs within a system's state. Although dissimated work is visible in a system's state, it is typically invisible in a state ensemble due to the randomization of a system's state during equilibrium measurements, which can be managed through controlled non-equilibration. A resolution is provided for Poincaré's recurrence theorem, which states that the internal microwork caused by an isolated system's state is accumulated over time until the system's state is reactivated, re-enabling reversible work at re-equilibration even after insurmountable macrowork has been concluded. A resolution is also found for the apparent insurmountable work found in simulation studies, which reflect the internal microwork done during non-equilibration and can be managed through proper selection of a system's reference state, which should be equilateral relative to the stimulated state, which relieves the system's state and results in the dissipated work appearing as the primary work found in simulation studies at re-equilibration.

We utilized high-resolution ALMA observations of the Star Forming Region in Orion to identify and quantify 10 molecular lines, including those from carbon compounds like CCH and CN, as well as water and cyclopentadiene. Cyclopentadiene exhibited a similar abundance to its stable isomer benzene in this shielded environment, with a ratio of 1.25 ± 0.24, contradicting the typical 10^-4 ratio expected in the interstellar medium. Notably, the ratio of (CCH/CN) lines for cyclopentadiene was 2.5 times greater than for benzene. Furthermore, cyclopentadiene's absolute abundance ratio to water was 1.4 times greater than expected. These discrepancies between the line intensities of carbon compounds and the absence of cyclopentadiene's ionized forms may be explained by its high reactivity and short lifetime. Our research emphasizes the significance of detecting and understanding the spectral characteristics of short-lived molecules within the interstellar medium.

The proposed approach enhances conventional attention mechanism in translation models by implementing a look-ahead method. This technique utilizes an encoder's preview of future input to guide the alignment of current future inputs at each decoding step. Our proposed look-ahead technique effectively enhances the performance of neural machine translation, particularly in low-resource scenarios. This technique works best when integrated with translation engines employing attention mechanisms, such as those based on the Bahdanan et al. architecture. Furthermore, the look-ahead method excels when utilized in combination with beam search decoding method.

This letter aims to convey an important message in a broader context. We advocate for a translational approach that would enable the successful adoption of grid computing and related high-performance computing technologies across clinically relevant areas, including telemedicine and telehealthcare. To achieve this, we propose a set of guidelines for planning and executing such adoptions. As an illustrative example, we explore the possibility of developing a nationwide cancer grid and discuss the associated challenges and opportunities it presents.

A new class of quasi-Hubble-based gravitational models is introduced, specifically tailored for early-universe cosmology, and a detailed investigation into their singularities, thermodynamic properties, and cosmic trajectories is conducted. One variation of this new model is found to effectively describe both primordial and Big Rip singularities, while another is capable of transitioning from power-law expansion to cosmological-singular behavior. The model's parameters can be inferred from observed data, with the coefficient of the model's viscosity term falling within a specific range, and the corresponding universe fill factor residing near $10^{-5}$. Furthermore, incorporating both gravitational and particle radiation is discovered to make the model's singular behavior irreversible.

This paper posits that peers significantly influence an individual's curiosity, yet current curiosity assessment tools do not reflect this, as they primarily measure an individual's internal drive to acquire new information. To address this, we devised a novel approach to quantify curiosity through peers, building on this concept, we present a new item in the Big Six inventory designed to evaluate curiosity among peers. Following the administration of this modified survey to over 500 participants, we utilized an econometric analysis to confirm that curiosity among peers has a notable impact on an individual's own curiosity, as well as other dimensions of their character.

We have developed methods for training non-stationary and differentiable Mat\'ern GP models on smaller data segments, facilitating their application in various learning settings. Our proposed approaches enable mini-batch training, a common technique in large-scale settings, and allow for non-conjugate models, a more flexible and accurate modeling option. Our results for the non-conjugate approach surpass current maturing methods for calculating the inverse of the precision matrix.

Urbanized road systems have resulted in extensive monitoring through various methods, with automated sensing becoming increasingly efficient using ridesourcing vehicles. However, unpredictable moves of such vehicles can limit the reliability and scope of sensing. To overcome this challenge, we propose an innovative approach that leverages optimization techniques to select the most effective ridesourcing vehicles for monitoring purposes. Specifically, we focus on determining the ideal Socratic question for choosing the best vehicle to answer an unanticipated query about traffic conditions. This approach involves identifying the most suitable vehicle that maximizes the likelihood of providing accurate and comprehensive answers to the query. We develop efficient algorithms to address these selections and validate them using actual data from ride-sharing companies, with our results demonstrating significant improvements in coverage and reliability.

If dark matter interacts through a vector mediator that connects to a fermion like the tau, stringent limits on scattering with fermions can be bypassed due to strong constraints from $J/\psi \to \text{invisible}$ decays, but this also means that scattering with nucleons can face weaker constraints. As a result, cross-sections for dark matter scattering with nucleons through this type of mediator can be quite small, typically in the range $10^{-39}$ to $10^{-44}$ cm^2 for mass ratios m(mediators)/m(J/\psi) greater than one. Despite this, certain regions of parameter space with moderate or large dark matter mediator masses contain rates that are not yet well-established experimentally and could potentially be discovered with existing or upcoming experiments like the SHiP dark matter detector.

Recent research into variable stepsize symmetric gradient near limits methods (SGLMs) has produced impressive outcomes in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.
Although several publications have explored the implementation of SGLMs at recent and predicted time steps, there is a lack of research into their application on nonuniform time step and spatial grids.
Our work aims to fill this gap by presenting a new approach to implementing SGLMs on nonuniform grids, specifically a scheme based on the minmod near limit.
We demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of this method through applications to two test cases: a running voter model and a supersonic gas cloud simulation.

The Modified Frog Jumping Social Algorithm (MFSSA) is the latest iteration of the Frog Social Algorithm (SSA), which is a stochastic optimization method belonging to the category of meta-heuristic techniques mimicking animal behavior. Like other members of this category, the SSA exhibits poor performance when tackling complex, high-difficulty problems. In order to enhance the capabilities of the SSA and achieve better optimization results, modifications to the SSA's internal workings were implemented in the MFSSA. These modifications include adjustments to the rule for frog leaping, which directly impact the efficacy of the algorithm. Test evaluations across 23 standard problem sets demonstrated that the MFSSA outperformed numerous other established optimization methods, including the SSA, in finding the global minimum value. Furthermore, this study explores the potential applications of the MFSSA in solving real-world problems, such as identifying patterns in data sets and solving image-related problems.

The task of essay scoring has been shift from traditional, human-powered methods to modern technology due to the advent of computing. Modern systems, including multiple-choice and written responses, are now facilitated by written feedback mechanisms that involve human writers providing peer input. This peer feedback, though beneficial, can induce anxiety and limit the number of pieces of feedback a writer can receive, thus impacting the quality of improvement. Research has shown that peer feedback provides high stability but variability increases with each additional round of input, making it crucial to balance the number of peers providing input. Surprisingly, computer models, now used to provide written feedback, and human evaluators, now used to score essays, exhibit extreme sensitivity and stability in their evaluations of a main essay despite significant fluctuations in peer feedback inputs, resulting in inefficient and uneven improvement for writers. This phenomenon, known as the 'flat plate effect,' is an example of deep learning models' insensitivity to irrelevant data and may offer a new direction for research into enhancing peer feedback's written responses' effectiveness.

Real-time monitoring of parameters including plasma electrons' temperature, polarization, and density is essential for linking visual indications to specific plasma source properties and facilitating process control. A novel approach utilizing a plasma vision sensor and advanced machine learning techniques has been developed to train models capable of predicting these parameters based on visual observations of the plasma. The study's findings demonstrate that support vector regression models can accurately predict both plasma electrons' temperature and density with an average error margin of less than 15% and 10%, respectively, when the plasma is operated under certain frequency, gas types, and flow rate conditions. The research's success highlights the potential of combining computer vision and machine learning to monitor plasma sources in real-time, thus reducing the need for expensive equipment and enhancing the efficiency of industrial plasma applications.

The success of biological control using nematodes depends on the
variability in their numbers and that of the insects they target. We developed
a mathematical model to examine how dispersal methods and environmental
factors influence the populations of both nematodes and insects. This model took
into consideration the effects of random fluctuations and periodic changes in
temperature on the distribution of nematodes released from a point source.
We derived a steady-state equation for the average distribution of nemathodes
and derived the conditions for their extinction. A key finding was that
clumping in nematode releases can lead to higher death rates in target insects,
while the average distribution results in a lower birth rate in those populations.
Additionally, we discovered that released nematodes tend to accumulate in
areas with favorable conditions for them, such as cooler temperatures.

Nuclear segmentation in histopathology images is crucial for cancer diagnosis, yet existing deep learning methods are hindered by memory constraints when processing large patches for high-pixel-density analysis. A new, compact W-shaped network architecture is proposed to overcome this issue, effectively identifying nuclei in broader image patches. This unique design achieves exceptional performance, accurately detecting over 97% of nuclei and matching top rankings in histopathology image analysis benchmarks.

This study examines the rank twists of local factors in the context of representations associated with odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups. It demonstrates that the combined rank of these twists is determined by the overall isomorphism of the representations, provided they share the same supercuspidal support.

A Hamiltonian path within a graph G = (V,E) is defined as an edge-disjoint union of m shortest cycles that together encompass every vertex in V. If G can be decomposed into such cycles, it is said to admit a Hamiltonian path. This property is not universal among graphs; however, many do possess Hamiltonian paths. A path cover of an graph is defined as the set of Hamiltonian paths whose starting points are located at the stationary vertices of G. Similarly, a Hamiltonian path index is defined as the minimum number of such paths required. Some research has been done to determine the Hamiltonian path index of specific graph types, such as Cartesian products of cycles and grids. We define a new parameter, the HP-index, which is the smallest possible extra edge that can be added to make a graph admit a Hamiltonian path. For HP-index to be applicable, the graph must be connected and not a complete graph. We calculate the HP-index of Cartesian products of cycles and grids.

Researchers are still investigating which cellular death method is most effective in treating lung tissue damage caused by SARS-CoV-2. Recent data suggests that many patients with COVID-19 exhibit a high frequency of inflammatory responses, indicating a potential propensity for type II inflammatory responses that drive necrotic and non-apoptotic forms of cellular destruction. In light of this, it becomes evident that inhibiting apoptosis may facilitate a more robust immune response, whereas the suppression of necrosis could have a detrimental effect. Building on these findings, we propose that existing anti-inflammatory medications, such as dexamethasone, might effectively impede apoptosis but have limited success in preventing necrosis. In contrast, we suggest that certain antiviral drugs, including remdesivir and lopinavir/ritonavir, have a favorable impact on cellular destruction by triggering a non-apoptotic form of necrotic death. By utilizing a mathematical model, we assessed the feasibility of these medications in managing COVID-19, and our results demonstrate that a lower occurrence of necrosis leads to an enhanced likelihood of recovering from the disease. Consequently, we conclude that antiviral drugs possess a more significant therapeutic value than anti-inflammatory drugs in treating lung tissue damage caused by SARS-CoV-2.

By analyzing data patterns, specific variables can be identified that offer actionable insights into system behavior, potentially improving future predictions. A class of algorithms achieves this by隐式地构建因果模型, 理解哪些信息对于预测系统响应是真正必要的, 这使它们能够在强化学习中从少数几次试验中迅速学习, 并将从目标任务中获得的知识迁移到相关任务上. 这些变量通常是目标任务的相关变量在其他任务中的子集, 这提供了一个显著的优势, 因为收集这种额外信息需要大量的样本, 而这些变量在相关任务中的观察数量要少得多.

The Michelson programming language is being utilized for the development of Ethereum-based contracts, and the HELMHOLTZ static analysis tool has been created to detect potential bugs in these projects. Although static analysis provides valuable insights, Michelson programs still undergo extensive manual testing, as Michelson's design does not offer inbuilt safety guarantees. This limitation is addressed by HELMHOLTZ, which was significantly upgraded to parse and validate Python programs, ensuring that any bugs introduced into the Michelson code are immediately apparent due to the rigorous checks enforced by HELMHOLTZ's internal type system.

Recently, deep learning breakthroughs have led to the adaptation of Neural Networks (NNs) to address various problems, including image recognition and pattern mining. Graph-structured data is another common data type, and researchers have developed Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to solve such problems. Despite the success of GNNs, current models vary greatly in their architecture, making generalization and optimal design challenging. This paper proposes a unifying perspective, viewing GNNs as a extension of conventional NNs (CNNs and fully connected NNs), with the latter two being special cases, and presents both a theoretical and practical framework for the study of GNNs. Analytically, we demonstrate the equivalence of the polynomial representations used in the proposed framework for GNNs and NNs, and practically, we propose a modified back-propagation algorithm that facilitates the efficient optimization of GNNs.

We investigate a one-loop effect in rotating "hairy" black holes, specifically those with non-abelian spin connections, in four-dimensional asymptotically flat space-time. In this setup, we find that the entropy of these black holes is composed of a semi-classical area term plus an additional contribution due to the CS-hair. Notably, the value of this hair entropy is analogous to one-half the central charge derived in standard Chern-Simons theory for black holes in anti-de Sitter space-time. Our research indicates that the efficacy of the one-loop approximation for this calculation relies heavily on the stability of the hair in question.

The consistent extension of global symmetries in quantum field theories is attainable through non-invertible symmetries, defined by operator algebra relations involving nonscalar operators that generate a specific ideal. Notable examples include the Veervoorst operator in 4d N=4 SYM and K$|$Higgs|H\rangle = 0 in linearized gravity. By analyzing the operator algebra and the properties of the generating operators, the associated symmetry can be fully characterized, allowing the derivation of non-invertible fusion rules following the general framework established by Bartsch, Giacomini, and Redlich.

Elastography is a technique used in medical imaging to image the mechanical properties of tissue non-invasively, primarily through the estimation of strain. Although various methods utilize varying levels of image information to calculate strain in different directions, they all share the same basic approach of estimating strain in different directions independently, resulting in the accumulation of errors. Although total variation regularization can reduce the accumulation of errors in the lateral direction, it also creates blocky artifacts in strain maps in that direction. Although several methods use the relationship between strain components from the continuity equation, they all use the estimated strain components as input and therefore cannot take advantage of measured data's inherent properties. In contrast, we propose a novel approach using a deep learning network to calculate strain components in all directions from the radio-frequency (RF) data directly. Our proposed method, based on a variation of the two-dimensional discrete cosine transform, utilizes a network that estimates a complex-valued vector corresponding to the gradient magnitude of the phase transformation between the pre- and post-deformation RF images. Utilizing this approach allows us to make accurate estimates of the axial displacement, which in turn, provides more accurate calculation of strain in all directions, and provides improved accuracy overall when compared to the current state-of-the-art methods, as validated through both synthetic and real experiments in realistic scenarios.

Pseudocodes play a vital role in the cognitive process of problem solving, problem representation, and issue resolution, leading to an insight that coding can be viewed as logical pseudocoding. Pseudocodes are therefore valuable for the analysis of problem-solving behaviors and the development of next-generation tools. This study introduces logical pseudocodes, a notion that integrates elements of logic to lift the P vs NP difficulty challenge, similar to how combining Turing Pseudocodes and natural language results in Turing-completeness and a natural solution to the P vs NP problem. Pseudocodes are therefore easily verifiable and secure, unlike current programming languages that inherently contain bugs and hacking vulnerabilities. This investigation also explores the connection between logical pseudocodes and computable logic, and how this line of thought might influence the understanding of consciousness.

Given a set $X$ of size $n$, and a Boolean lattice $\mathcal{B}(X)$ constructed from $X$, let $[r]$ denote the set $\{1, \dots, r\}$. A coloring is considered Boolean rainbow if every element within $\mathcal{B}(X)$ is assigned a unique color from the set $[r]$. The Boolean rainbow Ramsey number $brb(n, p, r)$ is defined as the minimum rank $s$ such that any Boolean rainbow coloring using r colors on the lattice $\mathcal{B}(X)$, where $X$ has size n, contains a substructure isomorphic to $\mathcal{B}(Y)$ with rank y, y, such that Y is a subset of X and all elements within $\mathcal{B}(Y)$ share the same color from the set [r]. In this paper, we establish an upper bound for $brb(n, n-p, r)$, namely $brb(n, n-p, r) \leq \lceil n - p + r - 1 \rceil$, for any positive integer r and any p less than n.

We developed an efficient method to create coarser approximations (coresets) for the $k$-means clustering problem. Our algorithm takes nearly $20^k$ less time than previous coreset construction methods. It can also run continuously on streaming data, using minimal memory ($\tilde{O}(k^{2.5}4^k + \text{original memory})$) and only one pass through the dataset. Unlike most coreset construction techniques, our method does not rely on maintaining candidates for the final solution.

This paper addresses the challenge of modeling scenarios in pursuit-evasion games, where multiple pursuers attempt to capture a single evader operating within a grid-based environment. Building upon prior work that applies game graph decomposition to reduce computational complexity, we conduct a more in-depth examination of this technique when implemented on a grid world. We explicitly define a dynamic strategy for the pursuers, who lack immediate knowledge of their precise positions relative to the evader, but can access a list of predefined distance-based relations. Our results indicate a significant speedup in planning for complex scenarios, while also revealing an interesting correlation between the number of predefined relations and computational computation time. Additionally, we provide empirical evidence that this proposed method effectively enables the pursuers to achieve their objective in speedier scenarios.

Given nonnegative integers arranged in ascending order, we can create unique n-tuples based on circular shifts and decreasing sequences. If two such sequences produce identical results, the underlying integers must be identical or circular shifts of each other. A specific n-tuple is classified as nontransitive if it corresponds to a specific permutation pattern and does not contain certain subpatterns. This note explores the characteristics of nontransitive n-tuples by citing relevant research, focusing on a specific n-tuple that is compatible with a categorical scheme but does not have equivalent elements.

This research proposes an enhanced version of the cycleGAN model, which employs two AdaIN layers for AdaIN-cycleGAN. The two AdaIN layers respectively modify the feature maps produced by the generator and adjust the cross-correlation between the image domain and color space, thereby facilitating more effective learning of color space information. The two AdaIN layers respectively modify the generator's output feature maps and adjust the cross-domain correlation, which is critical for producing high-quality images in the target domain. The AdaIN design is particularly beneficial in scenarios where one of the image domains has a low resolution, as it is able to adapt to these limitations and still generate excellent results. The proposed model was evaluated on two datasets, which demonstrated the ability of the AdaIN design to significantly outperform the conventional cycleGAN model, resulting in the production of more accurate and detailed images in the target domain.

In this research, we examine representations learned in open-domain dialog systems from textual cues that give verbal encouragement. Traditional methods assess these representations by measuring how accurately they can filter out candidates in a view that was not seen. We investigate a new score function across multiple views, rather than just one. We examine our approach from two angles: first, we manually test it to understand how well representations are learned and the challenges they face; second, we propose a encoding method building on this, which we empirically show performs exceptionally well in a dialog encouragement task.

In this research, we analyze a specific second-order elliptic equation, which results from combining the $\eta$-Ricci-Yamabe and Laplace equations. The $\eta$-Ricci tensor is here defined based on the potential $\eta$-conformal vector $X$. Our main objective is to express both the divergence and higher order volume integral of the $p$-Laplacian in an $n$-dimensional complete manifold with no boundary, where this manifold is $\eta$-Ricci-Yamabe rigid with respect to the potential $\eta$-conformal vector $X$. This expression is in terms of the dimension $n$, the $\eta$-Ricci-Yamabe rigid constant $\delta$, and various parameters including $C_1$, $C_2$, $\tau$, $t_0$, $t$, $\lambda$, $\lambda_0$, $\eta$, and $\eta_0$. Furthermore, under particular conditions, our main theorem reduces to previously established results obtained by different researchers.

A new approach to calculating energies in deformed halos is introduced, based on a geometric interpretation of the Coulomb-trapped ion model. By linearizing the rotation of Coulomb wells, we can account for Coulomb energies in ion clusters and calculate angular momentum and shape deformations. Applying this method to Ne-90 and Ca-48 with various ion configurations, our calculated equilibrium deformations and rotational properties align with previous shell-model studies, demonstrating that Coulomb forces play a crucial role in determining the spatial arrangement of ions in ground and excited states, and by extension, the overall density distribution of nuclear states.

One key issue with video-enhancement models is their struggle to synchronize the frames and track the motion of objects within the video. To enhance object tracking and synchronize the video frames, BasicVSR utilizes an external tracker and an additional encoder, which reduces their efficiency and consistency for the tracking results. We propose BasicVSR++, a single-stage video-enhancement model that integrates a spatial-temporal encoder and a decoding module, successfully synchronizing the video frames and tracking objects within the model. BasicVSR++ uses spatial-temporal encoder branches that integrate multiple encoders and deconvolutions, reducing their size and tracking errors while enhancing consistency and efficiency. When compared to BasicVSR, BasicVSR++ shows superior performance, delivering a 0.52dB improvement in PSNR and enhancing efficiency by 13x.

This study addresses the challenge of describing processes involving V (where V represents W, Z, or a photon) in parton collisions at a given scale, taking into account corrections related to the electroweak force. By leveraging vector current conservation and utilizing the leading order QCD relation between lepton and hadron distribution functions, we establish a connection between parton distributions and vector PDFs in the limit of very high momentum transfer. Furthermore, a method is developed to determine lepton and hadron distribution functions based on the principle of factorization, which also allows us to express quark and gluon PDFs in terms of the relevant distribution functions at a given momentum fraction, in the context of the strong force's one-loop approximation. Furthermore, a direct relationship between the quark and antiquark distributions of the W and Z bosons has been established in the context of perturbative QCD at a certain order. As a result, the parton distribution functions (PDFs) for the W and Z bosons exhibit non-zero values for quark-antiquark pairs at a certain level of precision, which has significant implications for understanding the behavior of these subatomic particles in particle collisions.

This work explores model-based reinforcement learning with multiple learned dynamics models, showcasing its effectiveness in handling noisy measurements and data-corrupted states, as seen in a challenging robot juggling task. By leveraging several models, it demonstrates the risk of a solitary learned model's over-optimistic performance, highlighting the importance of incorporating diversity, as measured by the Jensen-Shannon divergence, into model selection. Through experimentally controlling diversity among models, a potential remedy is identified - sharing the fundamental dynamics across models while allowing for variation in state representations, whichAs model-based reinforcement learning (MRL) excels in sample efficiency and leveraging high-quality sensors, its real-world application is hindered by noisy and imperfect models. Especially in multi-task learning scenarios, where tasks are often acquired sequentially, model inaccuracies can propagate, degrading overall performance. Rather than relying on a singular learned model per task, a robust approach is proposed that employs a collection of models, drawn from a specific family, for each task. By addressing issue of correlated optimistic evaluations, this method allows for the simultaneous learning of multiple policies and models, leading to the development of a reliable policy that generalizes well across tasks. A key aspect of this approach is the incorporation of a diversity-promoting reward to ensure the coexistence of distinct models. Notably, it does not necessitate precise task representations, as the method can operate with abstract states. Moreover, the proposed approach leverages high-fidelity sensors for simulation-to-real transfer. Sharing the model family across

We examine a noncompact geometric space with compact edges, and analyze an equation whose solutions must remain consistent across these boundaries. Under specific conditions, we establish the parabolicity of this space and the existence of a specific function type solution. Furthermore, we establish a criterion for the presence of nonnegative solutions that do not vanish at the edges, thereby ensuring the existence of functions with specified boundary behaviors. Similar results are also derived for functions that remain bounded within these limits.

Godel's 1931 incompleteness discovery demonstrated that certain fundamental systems of arithmetic cannot be fully characterized by a single first-order logical axiom system. This discovery was later expanded in Godel's 1968 work, Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem has an even more profound implication. However, Rosser in 1936 developed a model of Godel's sentence based on an enhanced requirement for self-referential statements, which required the statement to be either true or false. This requirement was crucial for establishing that the statement cannot be proven false within the given system, thus demonstrating its unprovability. In this study, we replace the requirement that the statement must be either true or false with the condition that the statement implies the inconsistency of the given formal system, which we show can also be used to demonstrate the unprovability of the statement within the same system, thus generalizing both Godel's and Rosser's original theorems.
This study provides concise proofs of two fundamental concepts for monogenic functions in more than one dimension: Hadamard's three circles theorem and Bohr's inequality.

When planning a survey, researchers often need to choose a balanced random sample from the population, which is typically done manually using complex criteria. The author of this paper introduces a new algorithm that can automatically select a balanced sample with just a few simple steps. Additionally, the author compares the previous method with the new algorithm and provides an example to illustrate its effectiveness.

Recent advancements in deep learning have excelled in various vision tasks, notably when direct regression is pitted against classical methods that model tasks as optimization problems. Unexpectedly, direct regression has been underutilized in the realm of camera calibration, particularly for computing essential and fundamental matrices. To address this shortcoming, we propose a novel approach that utilizes computed metrics directly, eliminating the need for constraint optimization. Our method excels particularly in scenarios with limited correspondences and varying levels of image noise. To further validate its effectiveness, we examine our method's performance on the more complex problem of self-calibration from single images. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach when compared to the computed-then-optimized approach, especially in scenarios with limited correspondences and varying levels of image noise. Additionally, our method outperforms prior solutions on the standard self-calibration benchmark, particularly in scenarios involving corresponding images.

After receiving observed evidence, professionals in various fields, such as medicine and law, often need to produce multiple potential outcomes or "hypothetical images" based on these observations, commonly referred to as "posterior samples." To facilitate this task, we propose utilizing a Regularized Conditional Wassertein GAN (RCWGAN) model. Through a series of experiments using simulated data, real chest X-rays, and MRI images, we demonstrate that our method can generate high-quality posterior samples across a range of tasks and conditions. Notably, our approach has a distinct advantage: it does not require re-running a computationally intensive process for each parameter of interest, making it particularly useful when generating a large number of posterior samples.

This study provides characterization criteria for linear subspaces within fractional order systems, defined by Riemann-Liouville differential operators. We derive a general formula for invariant subspaces and demonstrate how this can be used to determine the specific subspaces that remain unchanged under the action of the system. A key condition for these invariant subspaces is related to their relationship with the domain of the system's operator. As part of this analysis, we also consider two distinct approaches to controlling linear systems, focusing on how controllability subspaces and the dual of unreachable subspaces relate to the system's overall behavior. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this work on systems where the starting point is zero and the unreachable subspace's properties. Additionally, this study extends its findings to systems that start with non-zero initial conditions, providing a more comprehensive insight into the behavior of these complex systems. We also draw parallels between the findings and their applications to systems that are easier to control or have difficult-to-reach unreachable subspaces.

In this study, we investigate a multi-hop Terahertz (THz) relay communication system operating in an environment with one user, an optimal number of finite THz antennas on a mobile vehicle, and an ideal base station. By examining the optimal beam training protocol, we derived the system's optimal outage probability. Key inclusions in this analysis are the impact of finite antenna counts on THz navigation, the effect of selecting the optimal beam training protocol, and the effect of random channel variations on THz system performance. By comparing our findings to existing studies on traditional systems, we observed that the optimal beam training protocol significantly enhances the performance of multi-hop THz links and improves the efficiency of their operation. By deriving the performance distribution of the optimal beam training protocol, we found that its performance can be expressed in a simple form, and that the optimal beam training protocol yields a more efficient expression than its non-optimal counterpart, resulting in a substantial improvement in system performance and overall efficiency.

The pulsar radio source of B1133.6+16 is subject to scattering in the interstellar medium between the Earth and the Neptune's hydrogen cloud. Using the Very Large Array at 4.85 GHz, scientists performed high spatial and temporal resolution observations of individual scattering screens. They identified 10 separate screens at distances ranging between 258 and 1,065 parsecs. The screen with the shortest path length was found to be located approximately 250 parsecs before the pulsar. The Faraday rotation angle of this screen accounted for about 60% of the total rotation angle between the Earth and the Neptune's hydrogen cloud. The results suggest that the scattering screen is widely distributed and contains ionization filaments with circular cross-sections, which are common among long-path-angle pulsars. The findings also imply that the interstellar scattering is composed of positive and negative rotation measures, supporting the 'swarm model'.

In this study, we investigate how cascaded convolutional encoder architectures, commonly used in image processing, can effectively capture the quasi-periodic nature of speech through modeling. Our proposed cascaded convolutional encoder (CCE) model excels in learning the inherent relationships within speech signals' glottal residuals, exploiting the quasi-periodic characteristics through separable modeling. Our approach leverages the inherent hierarchical structure of cascaded encoders to further explore speech's complex relationships. We establish a new benchmark using the MGCN speech synthesis dataset and demonstrate the CCE's superior performance, outperforming the molecular graph convolutional network (MGCN) by a significant margin in terms of Mean Square Error (MSQ) and perceptual evaluation measurement (PESQ) metrics. Our proposal's potential to efficiently model quasi-periodic signals via deep learning architectures highlights the value of such models in signal processing applications.

When working with vast text documents, an annotator's effectiveness can be significantly enhanced by using a computer-aided tool. For instance, a single annotator using such a tool can process approximately 10 times more data than a human alone can handle in about 40 hours. To achieve this level of efficiency, the proposed system utilizes a specialized interface that leverages the capabilities of the Qwen-VL-Plus multimodal model through FastAPI, enabling the generation of initial, high-quality annotations that can be reviewed and refined by the human annotator. To further streamline this process, a specialized Python library has been developed, integrating the proposed system into the Web3int annotator platform, which is an open-source, cost-effective solution for web dataset collection and processing.

We've developed an analytical framework to assess the chemical makeup of planets within our system, focusing on those located in nearby systems andreceiving a moderate amount of stellar radiation. A statistical analysis was conducted on these planets, where we assessed how factors like temperature, water vapor, metal content, and electrondonation influenced the abundance of gases such as sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen compounds, and others. A graphical method was also developed to determine the relationship between gases in these planets, with our results showing that water and coaren't always directly correlated, especially in planets that aren't completely filled with rock, and that a moderate amount of rock doesn't significantly affect this correlation. Additionally, our analysis demonstrated that a planet's rock content significantly impacts the connection between coarenia, and that in planets that aren't completely filled with rock, a large amount of ammonia isn't necessarily a sign of a high abundance of water. A planet's electrondonation also affects this correlation, and that in planets that aren't completely filled with rock,a moderateamount of rock can actually help increase the levels of a compound such as h2so4. Finally, our analysis demonstrated that a planet's temperature significantly impacts this correlation, and that in planets that aren't completely filled with rock,a moderateamount of rock can have a significant effect on this correlation.

Our research demonstrates that a zero-energy peak caused by non-Majorana
contributions can be distinguished from true Majorana modes as it is sensitive to
temperature and dissipates above zero Kelvin. Additionally, we pinpointed the
peak's line shape to follow a Breit-Wigner distribution. Moreover, we found
that the peak's height and width are affected by temperature in similar
magnitudes.

Creating detailed maps of entire regions requires a significant amount of time and resources, particularly when it comes to gathering information about the condition of the roads. This task is especially labor-intensive due to the need to gather automated data from multiple sources. This task can be streamlined and made more efficient by utilizing a dataset generated from a single vehicle equipped with an automated system to extract the necessary information. Furthermore, this dataset is ideal for developing and testing methods to automatically extract this data from a single source, as demonstrated in this paper. Specifically, we focus on estimating the numerical rating of the condition of the asphalt surface of the roads. Initially, we classify the surface material, which then allows us to assign numerical values based on the degree of wear and tear. As a result, we achieve a level of accuracy of around 93% in our estimation. Furthermore, the method outlined in this paper is adaptable to other contexts and surface conditions.Human inspection of roads is a critical component of infrastructure maintenance, as it involves evaluating the condition of the roads and their surfaces. This task is typically performed by a single operator using a camera, which allows us to develop and test a model that can process the data from a single camera. Such a model can be integrated into driver assistance systems and also generate data for the task of making maps of entire regions from a single vehicle. Furthermore, we evaluate our model on the task of assessing the condition of the roads and their surfaces, which is a critical component of infrastructure maintenance.

Brian Day's investigation into the bicategorical properties of shape theories reveals that topological Hochschild homology (THH) forms a coherent and universal shadow within this framework. As a result, THH can be regarded as the most robust incarnation of shape theory available, possessing the capability to capture insights across a wide range of contexts.

Recently, end-to-end neural networks have excelled in end-to-end source music classification (MISC). The current state-of-the-art in this field has been largely determined by Donmuslu and Saygin's research, utilizing the Magenta dataset. Their mixed training approach, employing a VGG-style architecture, achieved the best results to date with a 61.5% mean accuracy on the evaluation set. Despite these advancements, the size of available MISC datasets remains a limiting factor, hindering comprehensive evaluation of current models' performance. Existing source vs. non-source classification studies, including those in Donmuslu-Saygin, have utilized the small Magita dataset, which consists of only 0.5s of source music. This study introduces VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS), a new benchmark in MISC. It substitutes the VGGMusic dataset with the larger, larger-brained portion and contrasts it with the non-source music. Through a two-battle training method, employing the larger VGGMusic data and the non-source music, we achieved 80.3% mean accuracy on the evaluation set, surpassing previous research. This study demonstrates the necessity of a larger MISC dataset, which is crucial for evaluating the current models' performance.

Hyperslab Graph Convolutions (HS-GCN) is a novel approach that combines the benefits of the Lorentzian metric system, which provides a mathematically precise representation of hyperbolic space. Unlike previous variable-based node feature methods in hyperbolic graph neural networks (GNNs) that result in distorted representations due to the limitations of the Lorentzian metric, our method encodes Euclidean values within the hyperbolic framework. By leveraging the causal two-sheeted structure of the Lorentzian metric's representation, HS-GCN not only delivers an efficient and accurate node feature method for hyperbolic GNN tasks, but also outperforms previous embedding-based methods. Additionally, HS-GCN is adaptable to arbitrary hyperbolic geometries, making it a versatile tool for a wide range of graph gleaning (GL) applications.

This study investigates the recoverability of a distributed source term within an equation for the damped wave operator in a bounded domain. The domain is governed by two boundary control functions. Our primary objective is to demonstrate the uniqueness of this source term when the boundary controls and observed data are known in a restricted subregion of the domain. These data must satisfy an inequality for observability, which is crucial for the stability results in this study. An alternative approach to proving these stability outcomes is the use of a compactness-uniqueness argument. The findings of this research have implications for solving an inverse problem of determining a spatially varying parameter within the equation.

We v. 2/3 of the mechanical mode's population is transferred to a dark state, known as the TSS effect. This happens under specific conditions, which can vary widely due to large tuning ranges of the flux bias. The condition for TSS can also be observed through the absence of a corresponding peak in the quantum state of the mechanical mode. We show this behavior through a parametric sweep of the flux bias in a hybrid system. A significant shift in the optically accessible frequency of the mechanical mode indicates the onset of TSS. This shift can vary over a huge range, making it easy to realize the condition for TSS.

We investigate the properties of $ \nu $-calculus with unaries through modifications other than adjustments to identity and comparison operations, demonstrating that these changes result in a more complex formalism with heightened expressive capabilities and a coNP-satisfiability status, akin to LTL with unaries and weak temporal operators.

Social interactions are typically analyzed using statistical physics, and although many are adequately described by the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, some systems require the broader Tsallis distribution due to their non-additive nature. This study proposes an interpretation of the famous power-law form of the Tsallis distribution through a fundamental question: What occurs when money is exchanged in a closed system? By examining a straightforward model where two individuals trade with an average fund determined by the Talley factor, we successfully derive the Tsallis distribution, and as a result, we are able to examine key issues like extreme wealth, wealth distribution, and wealth concentration within these systems.

In the cosmological context, we examine linearized gravity on an FLRW background that includes a mass term, which alters the number of degrees of freedom. The gravity equation then determines the scalar mode mass and eliminates it from gravitational wave calculations, where the two remaining modes behave like a massive system. We analyze two theories: the standard massive gravity with a massive Stueckelberg field and a new gravity model with an extra vector field that successfully generates a massive graviton. In both cases, we explore how these theories relate to the "big three" theories of massive gravity. For the scalar case, we show that all three types of massive gravity can be derived, but in the case of a massive graviton, only two of the three types can be achieved. Furthermore, we show that some vector-based theories of gravity with a cosmological constant can be rescaled to include a universal term representing the cosmological constant. For each case, we derive the vacuum field equations in the presence of a general cosmological constant.

For any graph $G$ and its associated signed graph $\Sigma(G)$, an $n$-fold extended cover $\hat{D}_m(G)$ of $G$ can be m-folded. We examine the planar properties of these extended covers in four specific cases: (1) the double cover 2DG of a signed graph $\Sigma(G)$ is planar if and only if its vertex number is less than or equal to 4, (2) the double cover $\hat{D}_m(G)$ is planar for an odd number of vertices $m$ if its vertex number is less than or equal to 4, (3) an explanatory definition of a conjecture stating that all extended double covers $\hat{D}_m(G)$ are planar if the original graph $G$ can be drawn in a plane, and (4) an exploration of non-regular double covers $\hat{D}_m(G)$ and suggestions for further research.

We examine continuous symmetries under which a Hamiltonian remains unchanged, and classify quantum equilibrium states for such systems into four categories: those invariant to the symmetry, those grouped by the system's spin, those dictated by the symmetry's magnitude, and those unaffected by either the system's spin or the symmetry's magnitude. We develop joint classification methods by combining both types of dynamics and identify specific models representing each category of equilibrium states.

The notion of negative temperature can be effectively demonstrated within a two-level system and is accompanied by counterintuitive properties. Although often regarded as a theoretical concept, the idea of a system with a negative temperature is applicable to the study of systems with a finite number of states. This study is designed to facilitate a understanding of the negative temperature concept and provides the criteria for a system that exhibits negative temperature. Notably, the physics of a quantum spin system is highly complex, which complicates the analysis; as a result, we present the discussion in terms of probabilities rather than entropy.

We examine how the arrangement of finite integer collections impacts their restricted signed sumsets, with specific attention to linearly ordered sets and sums modulo n. Our analysis demonstrates that an optimal reduced summand can generate unusually large restricted signed sumsets when one particularly large integer significantly exceeds the others in a linearly ordered set. Additionally, we relate this phenomenon to specific, recently studied problems involving signed sumsets modulo n.

Deformable neural networks have demonstrated exceptional effectiveness in various image processing tasks, including medical image analysis and organ segmentation from abdominal CT scans. Building on this success, our research employs a deformable neural network to perform colorectal adenoma classification and grading, achieving high accuracy in overall classification, subadenoma level classification, and grading tasks. By utilizing the Deformable Adenoma Encoder-Decoder neural network, our model exhibits exceptional performance with a low loss value of 0.199 and a high accuracy of 94%. Furthermore, by analyzing the activation maps of the network, we gain insight into its decision-making process, revealing its focus on key features such as the stalk of the adenoma for correct classification. Our Deformable Adenoma Encoder-Decoder neural network outperforms traditional flat neural network approaches in terms of accuracy, marking a significant advancement in automated colorectal adenoma classification and grading.

This study develops a novel multivariate Galerkin technique to efficiently solve time-dependent problems, particularly those with high frequencies, in acoustic scattering. By leveraging asymptotic analysis, relationships between time-dependent and time-independent formulations are explored, facilitating reduction to a Helmholtz equation. Focusing on outwardly expanding domains at large radii, multiple scale expansions provide tailored basis functions. This approach yields significant performance improvements over conventional Discrete Harmonic Transform (DHT) methods in domains with rapidly expanding boundaries and addresses difficulties with reflected wave components at smaller radii.

Researchers collected and analyzed 40 ordinary chondrite finds from the Antarctic region in the 1990s and 2000s that were labeled as water-rich, initially reported to contain more than a few hundred ppm of water. To accurately compare these water-rich finds with water content of recent ordinary chondrite falls, which exhibited lower levels of hydrogen, the team adjusted for isotopic differences and found that the water-rich finds actually had comparable or even lower H2 content (up to an order of magnitude less) than falls Benenitra and Chelyabinsk. The study suggests that the previously reported "high water content" in these Antarctic finds was likely an overestimation due to previous measurement inaccuracies. Furthermore, the research indicates that the water-rich designation for these 40 chondrites is unnecessary and should be removed from their revised names. The study also briefly discusses the mechanisms behind the formation of water and hydrogen in the parent bodies of these chondrites.

This paper builds upon a previous study, extending the analytical framework used to examine key quantities like scalar products, form factors, and expectation values in models related to the XXX/ZZ chain. Rather than repeating existing results, this work explores new ground by exploring more complex scenarios involving multiple representations and higher-genana graphs. Leveraging results formed in the initial paper as foundational knowledge, distinct expressions are derived both for expectation values associated with a multi-local spin operator within the higher-spin XXZ chain across various regimes and for multi-loop form factors distinguishing between two regimes in the same model.

This study investigates the challenges of speech translation when language resources are scarce, particularly in zero-shot and few-shot settings. We begin by examining the limits of existing zero-shot methods, which rely on text-based techniques and result in poor performance. We then introduce two novel approaches, spectral domain generation and artifact-domain learning, that significantly enhance the proposed models and achieve groundbreaking outcomes, such as single-person performance close to that of task-specific recordings.

A new approach to describing a particle's response to radiation is introduced, describing its multipole moments based on the number of photons involved. The method's advantages over traditional multipoles are demonstrated, highlighting that electric/dynamic multipoles are particularly suitable for describing light scattering. This illustration is applied to spherical particles scattered by a single photon, revealing the scattering behavior of different multipoles. Notably, higher-order multipoles effectively describe the scattering, with a small contribution from odd multipoles, resulting in the scattering probability being dominated by even multipoles and photonic dipoles.

We establish a precise form of the Harish-Chandra isomorphism through the 
connection between Schur elements and shifted Schur polynomials, derived from 
determinant calculations of root values. This approach also leads to determinant 
formulas for double cosets in root systems and a minor expansion of Weyl 
denominators.

We apply an eggbox model, extending the standard setup with added dark sector fields, to analyze if dark parity symmetry can be maintained within a viable seesaw framework. By adding the dark sector, we find that the vacuum stability is enhanced to that of the Planck scale, while dark parity symmetry remains unbroken by radiative corrections, also up to the Planck scale. We determine the necessary dark sector parameters for dark parity stability, with implications for the scattering of dark matter in laboratory and cosmic settings.

In transition metal oxides, spin-orbit coupling significantly influences various properties, but its behavior is complicated by hybridization and can be described by a model that accounts for multiple sites and includes both exact and approximate expressions for the effective spin-orbit coupling strength. This study reveals that strong electron interactions and crystal field splitting must be considered together, and through comparison with experimental data in several compounds, the general principles behind this effect can be understood.

We extend previous work on the relative I-function of a toric complete intersection by examining a specific scenario in which one of its components is replaced with two smooth divisors D1 and D2 that are not intersecting in a toric variety X, forming a relative i-codimension 2 pair (D1,D2).  By leveraging the existence of a unique BPS spectrum for D1 and multiple potential BPS spectra for D2, we determine the relative I-function through sewing operations, resulting in an expansion of the original I-function with additional factors corresponding to D2.  This procedure illustrates the impact of different choices of quantum states on the result.  A physical interpretation of the outcomes in terms of four-dimensional N=1 gauge theories on a deformed conifold is also provided.

Deep generative models, which capture complex data distributions effectively, have significant potential when combined with appropriate image tools.  However, when applying this combination to medical imaging, it's essential to account for the latent code's influence on learned medical information.  Without considering this aspect, generators may mislead downstream tasks due to distorted data.  To address this problem, we propose using medical prior guidance based on task-specific encoders to understand images and codes within the domain of interest.  Our proposed framework maps images and specific attribute encodings into a shared latent space, where they can be effectively integrated through a combination penalty to ensure consistency.  Experiments conducted on Chest X-ray and CT chest images demonstrate that this approach successfully introduces new data capabilities and accurately enc medical information within generated images.  As a result, it improves the performance of downstream tasks such as generation and disease classification, and has the potential to introduce controlled medical information into generated images.  The source code for this project is available on GitHub.

Multidimensional data visualization is essential for essential decision-making in various fields, particularly in the economics and finance sectors. Although AI has made significant advancements in processing and presenting complex datasets, effective visualization for non-expert users remains a vital area of focus. To address this, we introduced an innovative, user-centered visualization technique called ViDaExpert and developed a specialized AI assistant, VdaExpert, to demonstrate our method. Through an engaging, interactive interface, VdaExpert provides multiple features, including real-time, engaging consultations, expert knowledge-driven suggestions, and seamless human-AI collaboration. Users can easily interact with this system through an intuitive web interface, as well as offline through an executable program, which has been successfully tested with over 100,000 users in engaging, real-world scenarios, as well as privately, as well as on YouTube, as well as in workshops, as well as in business settings. The positive feedback obtained from these sessions indicates that this system can produce visually appealing and engaging representations of intricate datasets, while also providing an intuitive and seamless user experience. The system's performance was further enhanced by optimizing the underlying reasoning framework, resulting in impressive, sub-second response times, even when processing large datasets. This study develops an efficient direct sparse approximation method for multivariate polynomial functions, leveraging a computationally monomial-order-based distance measure. A sparse approximation algorithm is created by creating an inverse problem and solving it for the inverse. A key feature of this method is that it requires only a single solution, regardless of the number of selected terms. Two approaches for generating a well-conditioned and representative dataset are provided. Initially, a high-order 2-D monomial approximation is used to generate data for one dimension of 1D. A theoretical analysis indicates this method results in a relatively small and invertible matrix. A data generation method based on numerical integration is also presented to produce a dataset with a small condition number. Numerical experiments show the algorithm is highly effective and space-efficient. A data structure is created to minimize memory usage, achieving an inverse computation cost of O(NlogN) and a memory usage of O(N) for N elements. Numerical experiments on the 1D Blasius equation and 2-D Navier-Stokes equations demonstrate the method's ability to accurately solve boundary value problems.
